rationale: B wins because it is more allergic to the exact fuzz that would get a founder in trouble: "what 'annualized revenue' means" and whether the license is actually open. A has strong shapes, but "Why would a company chasing an IPO give away its flagship AI model?" smuggles in "flagship" and makes the contrarian angle shinier than the facts allow. B's "Databricks gives its model away while revenue grows 60% — a test of where the money in AI actually sits" asks the same hard question without pretending we already know the model is core IP.
gaps_in_A: "$3B ARR disclosure" overstates the supplied fact. The update says annualized revenue, not ARR; private-company revenue language is exactly where sloppiness gets punished.
"flagship AI model" is invented. The update says new foundation model, not flagship, core product, or most valuable IP.
"late-stage private companies protect and monetize their most valuable IP tightly" is a useful tension, but A states it as a premise before proving this model is valuable IP.

The first and third angles are distinct enough, but "regulated industries don't want black-box AI" and "direct shot at the API-gated AI business model" lean on the same open-vs-closed proof stack; both need the same license and benchmark evidence.
gaps_in_B: "For banks and hospitals" is vivid, but the update only says regulated enterprises. It is a fair likely example, not a supplied fact.

"cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API" and "inside its own perimeter" are stronger than the facts provided. Good reporter instinct, but it needs customer or compliance proof before it becomes copy.
"closed-API vendors are actually losing regulated accounts" is properly framed as something to test, but it still raises a proof bar the update does not meet.
"proprietary frontier models are the core asset" risks importing the frontier-model debate into a Databricks release that only says foundation model.
